drills.q: Name the first six integer argument registers in System V x86-64, the first eight in AAPCS64, and where each convention's return value goes.
drills.a: System V x86-64: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 (7th+ spills to stack); return in rax (rdx:rax for 128-bit). AAPCS64: x0-x7 (9th+ spills to stack); return in x0 (x1 for a second word).

drills.q: Distinguish caller-saved from callee-saved registers and explain why the split exists.
drills.a: Caller-saved registers may be freely clobbered by a call, so the caller must save what it needs across it; callee-saved registers must be restored to their original value by the callee before returning. The split avoids every function saving every register on every call, dividing the bookkeeping efficiently between both sides.

drills.q: Why can a leaf function on ARM64 skip stack frame setup entirely while x86-64 always needs at least a ret?
drills.a: ARM64's bl instruction stores the return address in a dedicated register (x30/lr) rather than the stack, so a leaf function can do all its work in registers and return directly via lr. x86-64's call always pushes the return address onto the stack, so even the leanest function must execute ret to pop it back off -- there's no register-only equivalent since the call mechanism itself is stack-based.

drills.q: A release-build backtrace stops after two frames. Diagnose and give two fixes.
drills.a: Frame pointer omission (-fomit-frame-pointer, default at -O2+) repurposed rbp as a general register, breaking naive rbp-chain-walking unwinders past the last frame that still has one. Fixes: rebuild with -fno-omit-frame-pointer, or use a DWARF CFI (.eh_frame)-based unwinder instead of frame-pointer walking.

drills.q: A function misbehaves only at -O2, not -O0. What's the first hypothesis and how do you confirm it rather than blaming the compiler?
drills.a: Undefined behavior in the source (signed integer overflow, uninitialized read, strict-aliasing violation) that -O0's minimal transformation happened not to expose but -O2's aggressive analysis/transformation does. Confirm with -fsanitize=undefined,address (UBSan/ASan), which instruments these UB classes at runtime independent of optimization level -- compiler bugs are comparatively rare next to application UB.

drills.q: Mechanically explain why a naive CPython arithmetic loop is roughly 50-100x slower than the equivalent compiled C loop.
drills.a: Four stacked per-iteration costs absent in compiled C: bytecode dispatch overhead through the eval loop, boxed PyObject allocation for each arithmetic result (Python ints are heap-allocated, immutable structs with a refcount), reference-counting reads/writes on every object touch, and dynamic __add__ method dispatch instead of a single machine add. A compiled C loop is typically just a register increment/compare, possibly vectorized.

drills.q: Does 'Python is 100x slower than C' apply to all Python code? Explain the boundary.
drills.a: No -- it applies specifically to the interpreter loop's per-element overhead in tight pure-Python numeric loops. Code whose hot path executes inside a C extension (NumPy vectorized ops, most standard-library internals, database drivers) pays essentially none of that overhead, which is why vectorizing with NumPy or compiling with Cython/Numba fixes the problem rather than micro-tuning pure-Python arithmetic.

drills.q: Explain concretely what Windows x64's calling convention does differently from System V x86-64, and why this makes object code non-portable across the two even on identical hardware.
drills.a: Windows x64 uses only 4 register arguments (rcx, rdx, r8, r9 vs System V's 6), requires the caller to reserve a 32-byte shadow space on the stack even when all arguments fit in registers, and has a different caller/callee-saved register split. Object files compiled under each convention disagree about where arguments and saved registers live, so they cannot be linked together without an explicit calling-convention-aware shim, regardless of the underlying x86-64 hardware being identical.

drills.q: In objdump output, how do you tell whether a function call was fully inlined versus the target being dead-code-eliminated for an unrelated reason?
drills.a: Check whether the target function's effects (its actual arithmetic/behavior) are still present inline at the call site with no corresponding call instruction (inlined) versus genuinely absent along with the surrounding logic that would have used its result (dead-code-eliminated because the result was provably unused). Compiler Explorer's source-to-assembly highlighting makes this distinction visible directly; raw objdump requires manually correlating instructions back to source.

drills.q: Your team wants to enable -fno-omit-frame-pointer fleet-wide for continuous production profiling. Make the cost-benefit case, and note the alternative that avoids the runtime cost.
drills.a: Cost: a measurable but typically small (low-single-digit percent, workload-dependent) throughput regression from dedicating rbp to frame-pointer bookkeeping instead of general use. Benefit: perf-based (or equivalent) production profiling relies on stack unwinding to attribute CPU time to call stacks, and frame-pointer-based unwinding is far more reliable and cheaper per sample than the alternative. Alternative: DWARF CFI (.eh_frame)-based unwinding avoids the runtime register cost but is more expensive to compute per profiling sample and can be unreliable for hand-written or JIT-generated code lacking CFI metadata -- it's a different point on the same tradeoff, not a free escape from it.
